name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_NUCLEI_Q13_1 - Radioactive decay in containers after one half-life

questiontext.text: Suppose we consider a large number of containers each containing initially 10000 atoms of a radioactive material with a half life of 1 year. After 1 year,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Radioactive decay is a spontaneous, random, and probabilistic process at the level of individual nuclei. For any single atom, the probability of surviving one half-life \(T_{1/2}\) without decaying is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Each container starts with \(N_0 = 10000\) atoms and \(T_{1/2} = 1\text{ year}\). After \(t = 1\text{ year} = T_{1/2}\), the expected (mean) number of undecayed atoms in a container is \(\langle N \rangle = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/T_{1/2}} = 10000 \times \frac{1}{2} = 5000\).

Step 3: Application
Because individual decays are independent random events, the exact number of undecayed atoms in a given container fluctuates around the mean value of \(5000\) (following a binomial distribution). Some containers will have slightly more than \(5000\) atoms and some will have slightly fewer than \(5000\) atoms, so they will not all have the exact same count. However, by the law of large numbers, the average number of atoms across a large number of containers will be very close to \(5000\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The containers will in general have different numbers of the atoms of the material, but their average will be close to \(5000\).

answer.text: all the containers will have 5000 atoms of the material.
all the containers will contain the same number of atoms of the material but that number will only be approximately 5000.
the containers will in general have different numbers of the atoms of the material but their average will be close to 5000.
none of the containers can have more than 5000 atoms.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_NUCLEI_Q13_2 - Gravitational mass of a bound hydrogen atom

questiontext.text:
The gravitational force between a H-atom and another particle of mass \(m\) will be given by Newton's law:

\[F = G \frac{M \cdot m}{r^2}, \text{ where } r \text{ is in km and}\]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Einstein's mass-energy equivalence relation \(\Delta E = \Delta m c^2\), when particles combine to form a bound system, energy equal to the binding energy \(B\) is released, reducing the total rest mass of the bound system relative to the sum of the masses of its free constituents.

Step 2: Evaluation
A hydrogen atom is a bound system consisting of a proton of mass \(m_{\text{proton}}\) and an electron of mass \(m_{\text{electron}}\), with binding energy \(B = 13.6\text{ eV}\) in the ground state. The mass defect corresponding to this binding energy is \(\Delta m = \frac{B}{c^2}\).

Step 3: Application
Therefore, the effective mass \(M\) of the hydrogen atom that enters Newton's law of gravitation is the sum of the constituent masses minus the mass equivalent of the binding energy: \(M = m_{\text{proton}} + m_{\text{electron}} - \frac{B}{c^2}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The mass \(M\) of the hydrogen atom is \(M = m_{\text{proton}} + m_{\text{electron}} - \frac{B}{c^2}\) with \(B = 13.6\text{ eV}\).

answer.text: \(M = m_{\text{proton}} + m_{\text{electron}}\),
\(M = m_{\text{proton}} + m_{\text{electron}} - \frac{B}{c^2}\) (\(B = 13.6\text{ eV}\)).
\(M\) is not related to the mass of the hydrogen atom.
\(M = m_{\text{proton}} + m_{\text{electron}} - \frac{|V|}{c^2}\) (\(|V| =\) magnitude of the potential energy of electron in the H-atom).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_NUCLEI_Q13_3 - Effect of radioactive decay on electronic energy levels

questiontext.text: When a nucleus in an atom undergoes a radioactive decay, the electronic energy levels of the atom

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The electronic energy levels of an atom depend on the nuclear charge \(Ze\), i.e., the atomic number \(Z\) of the nucleus (for example, in a hydrogen-like model, \(E_n \propto Z^2\)). Any change in \(Z\) alters the Coulomb attraction experienced by the orbital electrons and thus shifts the electronic energy levels.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(\alpha\)-decay, the nucleus emits a \({}^4_2\text{He}\) particle, so the atomic number decreases by \(2\) (\(Z \to Z - 2\)). In \(\beta\)-decay (\(\beta^-\) or \(\beta^+\)), a neutron transforms into a proton or vice versa, so the atomic number changes by \(\pm 1\) (\(Z \to Z \pm 1\)). In \(\gamma\)-decay, an excited nucleus emits a high-energy photon to reach a lower nuclear energy state without changing either its atomic number \(Z\) or its mass number \(A\).

Step 3: Application
Because \(Z\) changes during \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) decays, the electronic energy levels change for both \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) radioactivity. Because \(Z\) remains unchanged during \(\gamma\)-decay, the electronic energy levels do not change for \(\gamma\)-radioactivity.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The electronic energy levels of the atom change for \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) radioactivity, but not for \(\gamma\)-radioactivity.

answer.text: do not change for any type of radioactivity.
change for \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) radioactivity but not for \(\gamma\)-radioactivity.
change for \(\alpha\)-radioactivity but not for others.
change for \(\beta\)-radioactivity but not for others.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_NUCLEI_Q13_4 - Q-value expressions for beta minus and beta plus decay

questiontext.text: \(M_x\) and \(M_y\) denote the atomic masses of the parent and the daughter nuclei respectively in a radioactive decay. The \(Q\)-value for a \(\beta^-\) decay is \(Q_1\) and that for a \(\beta^+\) decay is \(Q_2\). If \(m_x\) denotes the mass of an electron, then which of the following statements is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Atomic mass of the parent atom is \(M_x\), atomic mass of the daughter atom is \(M_y\), mass of an electron (or positron) is \(m_x\), \(Q\)-value for \(\beta^-\) decay is \(Q_1\), and \(Q\)-value for \(\beta^+\) decay is \(Q_2\). Let \(Z\) be the atomic number of the parent nucleus.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The binding energy of orbital electrons is neglected compared to nuclear energies, so the nuclear mass of a neutral atom of atomic number \(Z\) and atomic mass \(M\) is \(M - Z m_x\). The mass of a neutrino or antineutrino is taken as negligible, and \(Q = (\text{initial nuclear mass} - \text{final nuclear mass})c^2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For \(\beta^-\) decay: \({}^A_Z X \to {}^A_{Z+1} Y + e^- + \bar{\nu}\).
For \(\beta^+\) decay: \({}^A_Z X \to {}^A_{Z-1} Y + e^+ + \nu\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For \(\beta^-\) decay, the initial nuclear mass is \(M_x - Z m_x\), and the final mass of the daughter nucleus plus emitted electron is \([M_y - (Z+1)m_x] + m_x = M_y - Z m_x\). Subtracting gives: \[Q_1 = \left[(M_x - Z m_x) - (M_y - Z m_x)\right]c^2 = (M_x - M_y)c^2\] For \(\beta^+\) decay, the initial nuclear mass is \(M_x - Z m_x\), and the final mass of the daughter nucleus plus emitted positron is \([M_y - (Z-1)m_x] + m_x = M_y - Z m_x + 2m_x\). Subtracting gives: \[Q_2 = \left[(M_x - Z m_x) - (M_y - Z m_x + 2m_x)\right]c^2 = (M_x - M_y - 2m_x)c^2\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) have dimensions of energy (\(\text{mass} \times c^2\)), and \(\beta^+\) decay requires an additional \(2m_x c^2\) threshold compared to \(\beta^-\) decay in terms of atomic masses. Thus, \(Q_1 = (M_x - M_y)c^2\) and \(Q_2 = (M_x - M_y - 2m_x)c^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_NUCLEI_Q13_5 - Stability of triton against neutron decay

questiontext.text: Tritium is an isotope of hydrogen whose nucleus Triton contains 2 neutrons and 1 proton. Free neutrons decay into \(p + \overline{e} + \overline{\nu}\). If one of the neutrons in Triton decays, it would transform into \(\text{He}^3\) nucleus. This does not happen. This is because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A spontaneous nuclear decay process is only possible if it is energetically favorable, meaning the total energy (rest mass energy) of the initial nucleus must be greater than that of the final products (so that \(Q > 0\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
While a free neutron has greater mass than a proton plus an electron and therefore decays spontaneously, a neutron bound inside a nucleus is subject to nuclear binding energy. Whether a bound neutron can undergo \(\beta^-\) decay depends on the total energy difference between the parent nucleus and the daughter nucleus.

Step 3: Application
Based on the premise stated in the question, if the decay of a neutron inside Triton into \(\text{He}^3\) does not occur, it is because the Triton energy is less than that of a \(\text{He}^3\) nucleus, making the transition energetically forbidden.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Triton energy is less than that of a \(\text{He}^3\) nucleus.

answer.text: Triton energy is less than that of a \(\text{He}^3\) nucleus.
the electron created in the beta decay process cannot remain in the nucleus.
both the neutrons in triton have to decay simultaneously resulting in a nucleus with 3 protons, which is not a \(\text{He}^3\) nucleus.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_NUCLEI_Q13_6 - Neutron excess in heavy stable nuclei

questiontext.text: Heavy stable nuclei have more neutrons than protons. This is because of the fact that

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nuclear stability depends on the balance between the attractive strong nuclear force (which acts between all nucleons over a very short range) and the repulsive electrostatic (Coulomb) force (which acts between all protons over a long range).

Step 2: Evaluation
As the atomic number \(Z\) increases in heavy nuclei, every proton repels every other proton in the nucleus, so the total electrostatic repulsion grows roughly as \(Z(Z-1)\), whereas the short-range attractive nuclear force saturates and acts only between nearest neighbors.

Step 3: Application
To overcome this growing electrostatic repulsion between protons and keep the nucleus bound, extra neutrons are needed because neutrons are electrically neutral (contributing no Coulomb repulsion) while still providing attractive nuclear forces.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Heavy stable nuclei have more neutrons than protons because electrostatic forces between protons are repulsive.

answer.text: neutrons are heavier than protons.
electrostatic force between protons are repulsive.
neutrons decay into protons through beta decay.
nuclear forces between neutrons are weaker than that between protons.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_NUCLEI_Q13_7 - Why moderators in nuclear reactors use light nuclei

questiontext.text: In a nuclear reactor, moderators slow down the neutrons which come out in a fission process. The moderator used have light nuclei. Heavy nuclei will not serve the purpose because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a nuclear reactor, fast neutrons produced during fission are slowed down (thermalized) through elastic collisions with the nuclei of a moderator.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a head-on elastic collision between a particle of mass \(m\) (neutron) and a stationary target of mass \(M\) (moderator nucleus), the fraction of kinetic energy transferred to the target is \(\frac{\Delta K}{K} = \frac{4mM}{(m+M)^2}\).

Step 3: Application
When \(M \approx m\) (light nuclei such as hydrogen or deuterium), \(\frac{\Delta K}{K} \approx 1\), meaning a neutron loses almost all its kinetic energy in a single head-on collision. In contrast, when \(M \gg m\) (heavy nuclei), \(\frac{\Delta K}{K} \approx \frac{4m}{M} \ll 1\), so the neutron rebounds with almost its original speed and loses negligible energy.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Heavy nuclei will not serve the purpose of a moderator because elastic collision of neutrons with heavy nuclei will not slow them down.

answer.text: they will break up.
elastic collision of neutrons with heavy nuclei will not slow them down.
the net weight of the reactor would be unbearably high.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_NUCLEI_Q13_8 - Reasons why nuclear fusion fails at ordinary conditions

questiontext.text: Fusion processes, like combining two deuterons to form a He nucleus are impossible at ordinary temperatures and pressure. The reasons for this can be traced to the fact:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For two light nuclei (such as deuterons) to undergo nuclear fusion, they must approach each other closely enough for the attractive strong nuclear force to bind them together.

Step 2: Evaluation
First, nuclear forces have a very short range (on the order of \(10^{-15}\text{ m}\)), so the two nuclei must come within this tiny separation. Second, because both nuclei are positively charged, they experience a strong mutual electrostatic (Coulomb) repulsion as they approach each other.

Step 3: Application
At ordinary temperatures and pressures, the thermal kinetic energy of the nuclei is far too small to overcome this Coulomb potential barrier and bring them within the short range of the nuclear force. Extremely high temperatures (thermonuclear conditions) are required to supply the necessary kinetic energy.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The reasons are that nuclear forces have short range and nuclei are positively charged.

answer.text: nuclear forces have short range.
nuclei are positively charged.
the original nuclei must be completely ionized before fusion can take place.
the original nuclei must first break up before combining with each other.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_NUCLEI_Q13_9 - Condition for two radioactive samples to have equal decay rates

questiontext.text: Samples of two radioactive nuclides A and B are taken. \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\) are the disintegration constants of A and B respectively. In which of the following cases, the two samples can simultaneously have the same decay rate at any time?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Two radioactive nuclides A and B have disintegration constants \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\), respectively. Let their initial decay rates at \(t = 0\) be \(R_{0\mathrm{A}}\) and \(R_{0\mathrm{B}}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Time \(t\) after the start of observation satisfies \(t > 0\), and disintegration constants are positive (\(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}, \lambda_{\mathrm{B}} > 0\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The decay rate (activity) of a radioactive sample at time \(t\) is given by: \[R(t) = R_0 e^{-\lambda t}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Equating the decay rates of A and B at some time \(t > 0\): \[R_{0\mathrm{A}} e^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} t} = R_{0\mathrm{B}} e^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} t} \implies \frac{R_{0\mathrm{A}}}{R_{0\mathrm{B}}} = e^{(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{B}})t}\] Taking the natural logarithm gives: \[t = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}} \ln\left(\frac{R_{0\mathrm{A}}}{R_{0\mathrm{B}}}\right)\] For a positive time \(t > 0\) to exist, \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\) and \(\ln(R_{0\mathrm{A}} / R_{0\mathrm{B}})\) must have the same sign:
1. If \(R_{0\mathrm{A}} = 2R_{0\mathrm{B}}\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\), then \(R_{\mathrm{A}}(t) = 2R_{\mathrm{B}}(t)\) at all times, so they are never equal.
2. If \(R_{0\mathrm{A}} = 2R_{0\mathrm{B}}\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} > \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\), then both \(\ln(2) > 0\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{B}} > 0\), yielding a valid time \(t = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}} > 0\).
3. If \(R_{0\mathrm{B}} = 2R_{0\mathrm{A}}\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} > \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\), then \(\ln(1/2) < 0\) while \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{B}} > 0\), giving \(t < 0\) (not physically possible after \(t = 0\)).
4. If \(R_{0\mathrm{B}} = R_{\mathrm{A}}(2\text{ h}) = R_{0\mathrm{A}} e^{-2\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}}\), then \(\frac{R_{0\mathrm{A}}}{R_{0\mathrm{B}}} = e^{2\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}} > 1\). With \(\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} < \lambda_{\mathrm{A}}\) (so \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{B}} > 0\)), we get \(t = \frac{2\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}} > 2\text{ h} > 0\), which is a valid positive time.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, the two samples can have the same decay rate at some instant when the initial rate of decay of A is twice that of B with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} > \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\), or when the initial rate of decay of B equals the rate of decay of A at \(t = 2\text{ h}\) with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} < \lambda_{\mathrm{A}}\).

answer.text: Initial rate of decay of A is twice the initial rate of decay of B and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\)
Initial rate of decay of A is twice the initial rate of decay of B and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} > \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\)
Initial rate of decay of B is twice the initial rate of decay of A and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} > \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\)
Initial rate of decay of B is same as the rate of decay of A at \(t = 2\text{ h}\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} < \lambda_{\mathrm{A}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_NUCLEI_Q13_10 - Decay rate versus time graph for two samples

questiontext.text:
The variation of decay rate of two radioactive samples A and B with time is shown in Fig. 13.1.

Which of the following statements are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The graph plots the decay rate \(\frac{dN}{dt}\) on the vertical axis against time \(t\) on the horizontal axis for two radioactive samples A and B. Curve A starts at a higher initial decay rate than curve B at \(t = 0\), drops more steeply, intersects curve B at an intermediate time, and lies below curve B thereafter.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The magnitude of the decay rate \(R(t) = \left|\frac{dN}{dt}\right|\) follows the exponential decay law, and the steepness of the exponential curve reflects the magnitude of the decay constant \(\lambda\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The decay rate at time \(t\) is \(R(t) = R_0 e^{-\lambda t}\), and its rate of change with time is \(\frac{dR}{dt} = -\lambda R(t)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
At the point of intersection of the two curves, both samples have the same decay rate \(R_{\mathrm{A}} = R_{\mathrm{B}}\). At this point, curve A has a steeper negative slope than curve B, which means \(\left|\frac{dR_{\mathrm{A}}}{dt}\right| > \left|\frac{dR_{\mathrm{B}}}{dt}\right|\), and hence \(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} > \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\) (equivalently, the decay constant of B is smaller than that of A).
Before the intersection point, \(R_{\mathrm{A}} > R_{\mathrm{B}}\) (A decays faster than B). At the intersection point, their decay rates are equal (\(R_{\mathrm{A}} = R_{\mathrm{B}}\)). After the intersection point, \(R_{\mathrm{A}} < R_{\mathrm{B}}\) (B decays faster than A). Therefore, A does not always decay faster than B.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both conclusions match the plotted curves: the decay constant of A is greater than that of B, yet A does not always decay faster than B; equivalently, the decay constant of B is smaller than that of A, yet its decay rate becomes equal to that of A at a later instant.

answer.text: Decay constant of A is greater than that of B, hence A always decays faster than B.
Decay constant of B is greater than that of A but its decay rate is always smaller than that of A.
Decay constant of A is greater than that of B but it does not always decay faster than B.
Decay constant of B is smaller than that of A but still its decay rate becomes equal to that of A at a later instant.
